cards.q: What is the difference between .NET Framework, .NET Core and .NET 6/8/10?
cards.h: Framework = Windows house, Core = portable tent, .NET 5+ = one family where even numbers stay long.
s: .NET Framework is the old Windows-only version, and it now only gets fixes. .NET Core started as the cross-platform, open-source rewrite, and from .NET 5 onwards it is simply called .NET. Versions like .NET 6, 8 and 10 are long-term support releases with three years of support. In my project I moved our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10 so we stay on a supported runtime and get the performance gains.
cards.k: framework, core, versions, lts, runtime

cards.q: Value types vs reference types?
cards.h: Value = photocopy, Reference = shared Google Doc link.
s: A value type holds its data directly, like int, bool or a struct, and it is copied when you assign it. A reference type, like a class or string, holds a reference to an object on the heap, so two variables can point to the same object. Value types are good for small, short-lived data. I use structs for small immutable values and classes for business objects.
cards.k: struct, class, stack, heap, boxing

cards.q: How does async/await actually work?
cards.h: Waiter takes your order and serves other tables; he does not stand at the kitchen door.
s: When I await a task, the method does not block the thread. The compiler turns the method into a state machine, the thread goes back to the pool, and when the work finishes the method continues from where it stopped. This lets one server handle many more requests. In our APIs every database and HTTP call is async, so threads are free while we wait for SQL Server.
cards.k: state machine, thread pool, non-blocking, task, async, await, asynchronous, valuetask, configureawait

cards.q: Task vs Thread vs ValueTask?
cards.h: Thread = hiring a worker; Task = placing an order; ValueTask = order already on the shelf.
s: A Thread is an actual operating system thread, which is expensive. A Task represents work that will finish in future, usually running on the thread pool, and it is what we use with async and await. ValueTask is a lighter version for methods that often finish immediately, like a cache hit, to avoid allocations. In my day-to-day code I use Task, and ValueTask only in hot paths.
cards.k: thread pool, valuetask, task parallel library, async, await, task, asynchronous, configureawait, thread, threading, thread-safe, concurrency, lock, race condition

cards.q: IEnumerable vs IQueryable vs List?
cards.h: IQueryable = send the shopping list to the shop; IEnumerable = bring the whole shop home, then pick.
s: IEnumerable works on data in memory and filters it in C#. IQueryable builds an expression that the provider, like EF Core, turns into SQL, so filtering happens in the database. List is a concrete in-memory collection that is already loaded. So I keep queries as IQueryable until I have added filters and paging, and only then call ToListAsync, which avoids pulling whole tables into memory.
cards.k: linq, deferred execution, ef core, list, ienumerable, iqueryable

cards.q: Abstract class vs interface?
cards.h: Interface = job description; abstract class = half-built house you finish.
s: An interface is a contract that says what a class can do, and a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class can hold shared code and state, but a class can inherit only one. I use interfaces for dependencies, so I can swap implementations and mock them in tests. For example, all our SFTP libraries sit behind one ISftpClient interface, and I used an abstract base class for the shared retry logic.
cards.k: interface, abstract, inheritance, contract

cards.q: Explain SOLID with examples from your work.
cards.h: SOLID = Single job, Open door for new rooms, Liskov swap, Interface diet, Depend on plugs not wires.
s: SOLID is five principles that keep code easy to change. Single responsibility means one reason to change, open-closed means extend without editing, Liskov means a child class must work wherever the parent works, interface segregation means small focused interfaces, and dependency inversion means depending on abstractions. In my SFTP integration, each vendor library implements one interface, so adding a new library did not touch the business code.
cards.k: single responsibility, open closed, liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion, design principles, solid

cards.q: Which design patterns have you used in production?
cards.h: My code toolbox: S-F-R-D-O = Strategy, Factory, Repository, Decorator, Observer.
s: In production I have used Strategy and Adapter to put different SFTP libraries behind one interface, and a Factory to pick the library from configuration. I used Decorator to add retry and logging around clients without changing them. With messaging I used the Outbox pattern so events are not lost, and publish-subscribe with Kafka and RabbitMQ. I pick a pattern only when it solves a real problem.
cards.k: design patterns, strategy, adapter, factory, decorator, outbox, singleton, repository

cards.q: How does garbage collection work in .NET?
cards.h: Nursery (Gen 0), school (Gen 1), retirement home (Gen 2); big furniture goes straight to the warehouse (LOH).
s: The garbage collector frees memory for objects that are no longer used. It divides objects into generations: new objects are in generation 0 and cleaned up often, while long-lived objects move to generation 1 and 2 and are checked less often. Large objects go on a separate heap. Most of the time I don't touch it, but I dispose resources properly, and once I fixed a memory leak caused by event handlers holding objects alive.
cards.k: gc, memory, generations, dispose, large object heap, garbage collection, idisposable

cards.q: Delegates, Func, Action, events and lambdas?
cards.h: Func = function with a gift back, Action = just do it.
s: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. Func and Action are built-in delegates: Func returns a value and Action returns nothing. A lambda is a short way to write the method inline, and an event is a delegate that others can subscribe to but only the owner can raise. I use lambdas every day in LINQ and in minimal API endpoints.
cards.k: delegate, func, action, lambda, event, callback

cards.q: What is deferred execution in LINQ?
cards.h: A LINQ query is a recipe, not a cooked meal.
s: Deferred execution means a LINQ query does not run when you write it. It runs only when you loop over it or call something like ToList or Count. The good part is you can keep adding filters before it runs. The risk is running the same query twice by accident, so when I need the result more than once, I call ToList once and reuse it.
cards.k: linq, lazy evaluation, ienumerable, iqueryable, deferred execution

cards.q: How do you make code thread-safe?
cards.h: One key to the bathroom (lock); a bouncer counting guests (SemaphoreSlim).
s: To make code thread-safe, first I avoid shared state where possible, by keeping services stateless and using immutable objects. When sharing is needed, I use concurrent collections like ConcurrentDictionary, the lock statement for small critical sections, and SemaphoreSlim for async code because you cannot await inside a lock. For example, our CSV import used a lock row in the database so two users could not import the same study at once.
cards.k: thread safety, lock, concurrency, race condition, semaphoreslim, concurrentdictionary, thread, threading, thread-safe

cards.q: record vs class vs struct?
cards.h: Record = a receipt: two receipts with the same lines are equal.
s: A class is a reference type with identity, so two objects with the same values are still different. A record is mainly for data: it compares by value, is easy to make immutable, and has a nice ToString and the with-expression for copies. A struct is a value type that is copied, best for small values. I use records for DTOs and events, and classes for services and entities.
cards.k: record, class, struct, immutable, value equality, dto

cards.q: Exception handling best practices?
cards.h: Catch the ball only if you can play it; otherwise pass it to the goalkeeper (global handler).
s: My rules are simple: catch an exception only where I can actually handle it, otherwise let it bubble up to one global handler. I never swallow exceptions, I log them once with context, and I return a clean ProblemDetails response without exposing stack traces. I use specific exception types and avoid using exceptions for normal flow. In our APIs, one exception handler converts all errors into consistent responses.
cards.k: exception handling, try catch, problemdetails, global error handler, logging, exception, error handling

cards.q: Generics and constraints: why use them?
cards.h: Generics = one mould, many materials.
s: Generics let me write code once and use it with any type while keeping type safety, so no casting and no boxing. Constraints like where T is a class or has a parameterless constructor tell the compiler what the type can do. For example, I wrote a generic paged result type and a generic repository method, so every list API returns pages in the same way.
cards.k: generics, constraints, type safety, where t

cards.q: What did .NET 8/10 bring that matters for backend services?
cards.h: Upgrade = free horsepower plus a longer warranty.
s: For backend services, .NET 8 brought Native AOT for APIs, keyed services in dependency injection, TimeProvider for testable time, built-in resilience handlers, and IExceptionHandler. .NET 10 is the next LTS with C# 14 and more performance improvements. When I upgraded [3] services to .NET 10 in [early 2026], we saw about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency without code changes.
cards.k: .net 8, .net 10, new features, keyed services, native aot, timeprovider, c# 14, net 8, net 10, upgrade

cards.q: Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline.
cards.h: Airport security: each checkpoint can wave you on or stop you, and you come back through on the way out.
s: The middleware pipeline is a chain of components that every HTTP request passes through, in the order they are registered in Program.cs. Each middleware can do something before calling the next one and something after, or stop the request early. The order matters a lot: exception handling first, then HTTPS, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, and finally the endpoints. In my project I added a correlation-id middleware so every log line could be traced across services.
cards.k: middleware, request pipeline, request delegate, use, run, ordering, pipeline

cards.q: Explain DI lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped, Transient.
cards.h: Singleton = the office building, Scoped = your meeting room for one meeting, Transient = a paper cup.
s: Singleton means one instance for the whole application. Scoped means one instance per HTTP request, which is right for DbContext. Transient means a new instance every time it is asked for. The key rule is that a longer-lived service must not depend on a shorter-lived one, for example a singleton holding a scoped DbContext, because that causes threading bugs. In our services, DbContext and repositories are scoped and stateless helpers are singletons.
cards.k: di, dependency injection, lifetimes, singleton, scoped, transient, captive dependency, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime

cards.q: Controllers vs Minimal APIs?
cards.h: Controllers = full restaurant menu; Minimal API = food truck.
s: Controllers are the classic MVC way: classes with actions, filters and attribute routing, good for large APIs. Minimal APIs map endpoints directly in Program.cs with lambdas, with less ceremony and slightly better performance. Both share the same routing, DI and middleware. I use controllers for our larger domain APIs and minimal APIs for small services and health or internal endpoints.
cards.k: minimal api, controllers, mvc, endpoints, routing, minimal apis

cards.q: What happens at startup in Program.cs?
cards.h: Build the kitchen (services), lay the route (middleware), open the doors (Run).
s: In Program.cs, first the builder is created, which loads configuration from appsettings, environment variables and secrets, and sets up logging. Then I register services in the DI container. Then app is built, and I add middleware in the right order and map the endpoints. Finally app.Run starts the Kestrel server. Since .NET 6 there is no separate Startup class, everything is in this one file.
cards.k: program.cs, startup, host, builder, configuration, kestrel

cards.q: Filters vs middleware?
cards.h: Middleware = building security; filters = the receptionist on your floor.
s: Middleware runs for every request, early in the pipeline, and only knows about the HTTP context. Filters run inside MVC, around a specific controller action, so they know which action is being called and can see the model binding results. So I use middleware for cross-cutting things like correlation ids, logging and exception handling, and filters for action-specific things like validation or an audit attribute on certain endpoints.
cards.k: filters, middleware, action filter, mvc pipeline, cross-cutting, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: How do model binding and validation work?
cards.h: Bind = unpack the parcel, validate = check nothing is broken.
s: Model binding takes data from the route, query string, headers and body and converts it into my action parameters. Then validation runs using data annotations or FluentValidation. With the ApiController attribute, if the model is invalid, ASP.NET Core automatically returns a 400 with the errors. In our CSV import API, I validated each row and returned errors with row and column numbers so users could fix the file easily.
cards.k: model binding, validation, data annotations, fluentvalidation, apicontroller, 400

cards.q: How do you implement global exception handling?
cards.h: One safety net at the bottom of the circus, not one per acrobat.
s: I handle exceptions globally in one place instead of try-catch in every controller. In .NET 8 I use UseExceptionHandler with an IExceptionHandler class that logs the error with the correlation id and returns a standard ProblemDetails response. Known errors, like not found or validation, map to the right status code, and unknown errors return a 500 without internal details. This keeps every service's errors consistent.
cards.k: global exception handling, iexceptionhandler, problemdetails, useexceptionhandler, error handling, exception, exception handling

cards.q: REST principles, HTTP verbs and idempotency?
cards.h: Idempotent = pressing the lift button five times still calls one lift.
s: REST means treating things as resources with URLs and using HTTP verbs for actions: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to update part, and DELETE to remove. Idempotent means calling it many times gives the same result: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not. For POSTs that must not repeat, like creating a shipment, we use an idempotency key so a retry does not create duplicates.
cards.k: rest, http verbs, idempotency, get, post, put, patch, delete

cards.q: How do you version an API?
cards.h: Versioning = new edition of a book; old readers keep their copy.
s: I version APIs so existing clients don't break when the contract changes. The common options are a version in the URL like /v1, a query string, or a header. I prefer URL versioning because it is clear and easy to test. Mostly I avoid new versions by making only backward-compatible changes, like adding optional fields, and I create v2 only for breaking changes, with a deprecation period for v1.
cards.k: api versioning, v1, v2, backward compatibility, breaking change, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Configuration and the Options pattern?
cards.h: Layers of paint: the last coat (env vars) wins.
s: Configuration in ASP.NET Core comes from layers: appsettings.json, environment-specific files, environment variables and secret stores, where later sources override earlier ones. The Options pattern binds a section to a strongly typed class, so I inject IOptions of that class instead of reading strings. I also validate options at startup, so a missing setting fails the deployment immediately instead of failing later in production.
cards.k: configuration, options pattern, ioptions, appsettings, environment variables, validateonstart

cards.q: How do you do logging and tracing in APIs?
cards.h: Every request wears a name badge (correlation id).
s: I use structured logging with ILogger, so logs are key-value data, not just text, and they go to CloudWatch where we can query them. Every request gets a correlation id that is added to all logs and passed to other services, so I can follow one request end to end. For tracing and metrics we use OpenTelemetry and Grafana dashboards. This is how we find production issues quickly.
cards.k: logging, tracing, ilogger, structured logging, correlation id, opentelemetry, observability, serilog

cards.q: How do you improve the performance of an ASP.NET Core API?
cards.h: M-A-D-C-S: Measure, Async, Database, Cache, Scale.
s: First I measure, because guessing wastes time. Then I fix the biggest problems, which are usually in the database: missing indexes, N+1 queries, or loading too much data. I make calls async, add paging, use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, and cache data that rarely changes. For example, one shipment list query went from about [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds] just by fixing the query and adding a covering index.
cards.k: performance, optimization, caching, async, asnotracking, paging, profiling, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: What is CORS and how do you configure it?
cards.h: CORS = guest list at the door, checked by the browser bouncer.
s: CORS is a browser security rule that blocks a web page from calling an API on a different domain unless the API allows it. In ASP.NET Core I add a named policy with the exact allowed origins, methods and headers, and call UseCors in the right place in the pipeline. I never use allow-any-origin together with credentials. Our React app calls the APIs with a specific allowed origin per environment.
cards.k: cors, cross-origin, preflight, browser security, usecors, security, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cookie

cards.q: How do you make service-to-service calls resilient?
cards.h: Circuit breaker = the fuse box at home.
s: Network calls between services will fail sometimes, so I plan for it. I use IHttpClientFactory with resilience policies: a timeout on every call, retries with backoff for temporary errors, and a circuit breaker so we stop calling a service that is down. In .NET 8, AddStandardResilienceHandler gives this in one line. For work that doesn't need an immediate answer, I use messaging instead of HTTP.
cards.k: resilience, polly, retry, circuit breaker, timeout, httpclientfactory

cards.q: REST vs SOAP (WCF) vs gRPC vs GraphQL?
cards.h: REST = postcard, SOAP = registered letter, gRPC = phone call, GraphQL = custom order.
s: REST uses HTTP and JSON and is the default for public and web APIs. SOAP, which WCF used, is XML with strict contracts, still found in older enterprise systems. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and binary Protobuf, so it is very fast for service-to-service calls. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs. In my work we use REST, and I also maintained older WCF services.
cards.k: rest, soap, wcf, grpc, graphql, protocols, service contract

cards.q: How do you run background work in ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Background service = the night shift that keeps working after the shop closes.
s: For background work I use a BackgroundService, which is a hosted service that runs a loop alongside the web app, using a scoped service for each unit of work. For queued work I use Channels or a message queue. For example, our SFTP poller runs [every 5 minutes] to pick up vendor files. For heavy or scheduled jobs that must survive restarts, a separate worker or a scheduler is better.
cards.k: background work, hosted service, backgroundservice, worker, channels, scheduler

cards.q: How does EF Core change tracking work, and when do you use AsNoTracking?
cards.h: The DbContext is a teacher with a register: it remembers who changed.
s: EF Core keeps a snapshot of every entity it loads, and when I call SaveChanges it compares and generates updates only for what changed. That is change tracking. It costs memory and time, so for read-only queries, like list screens and reports, I use AsNoTracking, which is faster. I keep tracking for data I am going to update.
cards.k: ef core, change tracking, asnotracking, savechanges, dbcontext, entity framework, ef, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: Eager vs lazy vs explicit loading; what is the N+1 problem?
cards.h: N+1 = going to the shop once per egg.
s: Eager loading uses Include to load related data in the same query. Lazy loading loads related data automatically when you first touch it, and explicit loading is when you ask for it manually. The N+1 problem is when you load a list and then run one extra query per item, which kills performance. I avoid lazy loading in APIs and use Include or, better, a projection with Select to fetch only the columns needed.
cards.k: eager loading, lazy loading, explicit loading, include, n+1, ef core

cards.q: How do you manage EF Core migrations in a regulated environment?
cards.h: Expand, deploy, contract: build the new bridge before closing the old one.
s: In our GxP environment, the app never applies migrations by itself at startup. We generate idempotent SQL scripts from the migrations, review them like code, and apply them as a controlled step of the release through FV, UAT and production. Scripts are backward compatible with the previous version of the app, and they are kept as validation evidence.
cards.k: ef core migrations, sql scripts, regulated, gxp, deployment, idempotent, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: How do you handle concurrency conflicts in EF Core?
cards.h: Optimistic = check the version number on the ticket before you edit.
s: I use optimistic concurrency: a rowversion column on the table, which EF Core checks when it updates. If someone else changed the row first, EF Core throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. I catch that and return a 409 Conflict, so the user reloads and tries again. This avoids locking rows while users are editing, which is important for screens where two people may edit the same shipment.
cards.k: concurrency, optimistic concurrency, rowversion, dbupdateconcurrencyexception, 409, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: DbContext lifetime and thread safety?
cards.h: One DbContext per conversation; do not pass the phone around.
s: DbContext is designed to be short-lived and it is not thread-safe, so it is registered as scoped, one per request. You must not run two queries on the same DbContext in parallel, and you must not keep it in a singleton. In background services I create a new scope for each job. For high throughput, DbContext pooling can reuse instances safely.
cards.k: dbcontext, lifetime, scoped, thread safety, pooling, ef core, entity framework, ef, orm, migrations, linq to entities, thread, threading, thread-safe, concurrency, lock, race condition

cards.q: How do you run raw SQL or stored procedures safely in EF Core?
cards.h: Interpolated = parameterised = injection-proof.
s: When I need raw SQL in EF Core, I use FromSql or ExecuteSql with interpolated parameters, which EF Core turns into real SQL parameters, so there is no SQL injection. I never build SQL by joining strings with user input. Stored procedures are called the same way with parameters. I use raw SQL only for things LINQ can't express well, like some reporting queries.
cards.k: raw sql, stored procedures, fromsql, sql injection, parameters, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities, sql, sql server, query, index, t-sql, database

cards.q: How do transactions work in EF Core?
cards.h: All or nothing, and keep the door open for as short as possible.
s: SaveChanges already runs all its changes in one transaction. When I need several SaveChanges calls or other work to succeed or fail together, I use BeginTransaction and commit at the end. If retries are enabled for SQL Server, I wrap the whole transaction in the execution strategy. Our CSV import saves all rows in one transaction, so a failure halfway saves nothing.
cards.k: transactions, savechanges, begintransaction, execution strategy, ef core, rollback, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is WCF and what are its ABCs?
cards.h: ABC: Address, Binding, Contract = where, how, what.
s: WCF is Microsoft's older framework for building SOAP services on .NET Framework. Its ABCs are Address, which is where the service lives, Binding, which is how you talk to it, like HTTP or TCP and the security, and Contract, which is what operations it offers. I have maintained WCF services in my earlier work, and today the modern options are REST APIs or gRPC.
cards.k: wcf, soap, abc, address, binding, contract, service contract

cards.q: How would you migrate WCF services to modern .NET?
cards.h: Strangler fig: grow the new tree around the old one until it can stand alone.
s: WCF server is not supported in modern .NET, so I would move the services step by step. First I separate business logic from WCF so it can be reused, then expose the same operations as REST APIs or gRPC on .NET 8 or 10. If old clients still need SOAP, CoreWCF can host the same contracts for a while. We migrate one service at a time and test each one against the old behaviour.
cards.k: wcf migration, corewcf, grpc, rest, modernization, wcf, soap, service contract

cards.q: Walk me through how you upgraded services to .NET 10.
cards.h: I-T-F-T-P: Inventory, Target, Fix, Test, Promote.
s: In [early 2026] I upgraded [3] of our IRT services from .NET 8 to .NET 10, because .NET 8 support ends in November 2026 and a GxP product must run on a supported version. I updated shared libraries first, then each service, the tests and the Docker images. We compared performance during validation, released through FV, UAT and production with [no functional defects], and got about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency.
cards.k: .net 10 upgrade, migration, lts, story, .net 8, .net 10, net 8, net 10, upgrade

cards.q: Do you need Repository and Unit of Work on top of EF Core?
cards.h: Do not wrap a gift that is already wrapped, unless you need a label on it.
s: Not always. EF Core's DbContext is already a unit of work and DbSet already behaves like a repository. Adding a generic repository on top often just hides useful features like Include and projections. I add a repository only when it gives real value, like hiding complex queries or making the domain cleaner to test. In some of our services we have repositories, and in newer ones we use DbContext directly with focused query classes.
cards.k: repository pattern, unit of work, ef core, dbcontext, entity framework, ef, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?
cards.h: Clustered = the dictionary itself sorted A to Z; non-clustered = the index at the back of a textbook.
s: A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows, so a table can have only one, and it is usually the primary key. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points back to the row, and you can have many. A covering non-clustered index includes all the columns a query needs, so SQL Server doesn't have to look up the row. That trick fixed our slow shipment list query.
cards.k: clustered index, non-clustered index, covering index, include columns, sql server, index, indexes, clustered, non-clustered, composite index, filtered index

cards.q: How did you optimize a slow SQL query?
cards.h: C-P-F-M: Capture, Plan, Fix, Measure.
s: Our site shipment list was timing out for a big study, taking about [8 to 12 seconds]. I took the real query from Query Store and read the execution plan. It showed a full scan, key lookups and a CONVERT on a date column that stopped the index being used. I rewrote the date filter as a range, added a covering index and server-side paging. Reads dropped from about [400,000 to 2,000] and the time went to [under 300 milliseconds].
cards.k: sql optimization, slow query, execution plan, query store, covering index, story, sql, sql server, query, index, t-sql, database

cards.q: What does SARGable mean?
cards.h: Do not put the column in handcuffs (functions), or the index cannot run.
s: SARGable means the WHERE condition is written so SQL Server can use an index seek. If I wrap the column in a function, like YEAR of OrderDate or CONVERT, or use a leading wildcard in LIKE, SQL Server has to scan every row. The fix is to keep the column clean and move the logic to the value side, for example a date range instead of a function. That was exactly the fix in our shipment query.
cards.k: sargable, index seek, where clause, functions on columns, sql server

cards.q: Explain the types of joins.
cards.h: Inner = handshake, Left = left side keeps everyone.
s: An inner join returns only rows that match in both tables. A left join returns all rows from the left table, with nulls where there is no match, and a right join is the opposite. A full outer join returns everything from both sides. A cross join gives every combination. I mostly use inner and left joins, for example a left join to show sites even if they have no shipments yet.
cards.k: joins, inner join, left join, right join, full outer join, cross join, sql

cards.q: Normalization vs denormalization?
cards.h: Normalize for truth, denormalize for speed.
s: Normalization means splitting data into related tables so each fact is stored once, which avoids duplicate data and update mistakes. Denormalization means intentionally copying some data to make reads faster, at the cost of keeping copies in sync. For our transactional IRT data we keep it normalized, and for reporting we use denormalized views or read models so reports don't slow down the main system.
cards.k: normalization, denormalization, normal forms, database design

cards.q: Transaction isolation levels?
cards.h: Each level adds a stronger lock on the diary.
s: Isolation levels decide how much one transaction can see of another's unfinished work. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, Read Committed is the SQL Server default, Repeatable Read stops rows changing under you, and Serializable also stops new rows appearing, but with more locking. s: A topic is a named stream of events, like shipment-status. Each topic is split into partitions, which allow parallel processing, and order is kept only inside a partition. A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. So more partitions mean more parallelism, and we use the shipment id as the key to keep its events in order.

s: At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time, so it can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means it is never lost but can arrive more than once, which is the most common choice. cards.q: How do you make a consumer idempotent?
cards.h: Stamp each letter 'done' so you never act on it twice.
s: An idempotent consumer gives the same result even if it gets the same message twice. I do it by giving each message a unique id and storing processed ids in a table with a unique key, in the same transaction as the business change, so a duplicate is simply skipped. Another way is using upserts or checking the current state, for example ignore a status update older than what we already have.

cards.q: What is a dead-letter queue?
cards.h: DLQ = the lost-and-found box.
s: A dead-letter queue is where messages go when they can't be processed, for example after several retries or if the message is invalid. This keeps one bad message from blocking the queue or being retried forever. We monitor the dead-letter queue with alerts, look at why the message failed, fix the issue and then replay it.

cards.q: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
cards.h: Write the letter in the same notebook as the change; a postman collects it later.
s: The outbox pattern solves the problem of saving to the database and publishing an event reliably. In the same transaction as the business change, I insert the event into an outbox table. s: I'd first decide the key, like per user, per API key or per IP, and the limit for each. Then pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts, sliding window is smoother. For one server, ASP.NET Core's built-in rate limiter is enough. Across many servers I'd keep counters in Redis or use the API gateway. Rejected calls return 429 with a Retry-After header.

cards.q: What are the main OOP principles?
cards.h: A PIE: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation.
s: The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Encapsulation hides data behind methods, abstraction shows only what is needed, inheritance reuses behaviour from a base class, and polymorphism lets one interface have many implementations. In my SFTP component, all libraries implement one interface, which uses abstraction and polymorphism together.

cards.q: Explain encapsulation.
cards.h: Capsule: only the pill's surface is visible.
s: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data private and allowing changes only through its methods, so the object protects its own rules. For example, a Shipment class doesn't let anyone set the status directly. It has methods like MarkDispatched that check the change is allowed. This keeps the data valid and makes the code safer to change.

cards.q: Explain inheritance.
cards.h: The child gets the parent's toolbox.
s: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the behaviour of a base class, which is an "is-a" relationship. In C#, a class can inherit from only one class but implement many interfaces. I use it carefully, for real shared behaviour. For example, our SFTP providers inherit from a base class that has the common retry and logging logic.
cards.k: inheritance, oop, base class, derived class

cards.q: Explain polymorphism.
cards.h: Same remote, different TVs.
s: Polymorphism means one interface, many forms. The same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object. In C#, that's done with virtual and override, or with interfaces. For example, I call Upload on an ISftpClient, and depending on configuration it runs the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro version, without the calling code knowing which.
cards.k: polymorphism, oop, virtual, override, interfaces, object oriented, encapsulation, inheritance, abstraction

cards.q: Explain abstraction.
cards.h: Steering wheel, not engine internals.
s: Abstraction means showing only what a user of a class needs and hiding the details. An interface like ISftpClient only exposes connect, upload and download, while each library deals with its own complex details inside. Callers work with the simple idea of a file transfer, which makes the code easier to use, test and change.
cards.k: abstraction, oop, interface, hiding complexity

cards.q: Class vs object?
cards.h: Cookie cutter vs cookie.
s: A class is the blueprint, it defines the properties and methods. An object is an actual instance created from that class at runtime, with its own data in memory. For example, Shipment is the class, and each shipment loaded from the database is a separate object.
cards.k: class, object, instance, oop

cards.q: Method overloading vs overriding?
cards.h: Overload = more options; override = replace.
s: Overloading means the same method name with different parameters in the same class, and the compiler picks the right one at compile time. Overriding means a derived class provides its own version of a virtual method from the base class, and the right one is chosen at runtime based on the actual object. So overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime polymorphism.
cards.k: overloading, overriding, polymorphism, compile time, runtime

cards.q: virtual vs override?
cards.h: Virtual = may be replaced; override = replaced.
s: The virtual keyword on a base class method says derived classes are allowed to replace it. The override keyword in the derived class actually replaces it. Then even if I call the method through a base class reference, the derived version runs. Without virtual, the method can't be overridden.
cards.k: virtual, override, polymorphism, inheritance

cards.q: new vs override, and what is method hiding?
cards.h: Override = real replacement; new = a disguise.
s: Override replaces a virtual method, so the derived version runs even through a base reference. The new keyword hides the base method instead: if I call through a base reference, the base version runs, and through the derived reference, the new one runs. That's method hiding, and it is usually confusing, so I avoid it and treat that compiler warning as an error.
cards.k: new keyword, method hiding, override, inheritance

cards.q: What is a sealed class, and a sealed method?
cards.h: Sealed = end of the family line.
s: A sealed class can't be inherited, which protects its design and can even let the runtime optimise calls. A sealed method is an override that stops further overriding in deeper classes. I seal classes by default when they aren't designed for inheritance, like most of our service classes.
cards.k: sealed class, sealed method, inheritance

cards.q: Stack vs heap?
cards.h: Stack = sticky notes on your desk; heap = warehouse with a cleaner.
s: The stack stores method calls and their local variables, it's very fast and is cleared automatically when the method returns. The heap stores objects created with new, which live until the garbage collector removes them. Reference types live on the heap, while value types live wherever they are declared, so a local int is on the stack but an int field of a class is on the heap.
cards.k: stack, heap, memory, value types, reference types

cards.q: What is boxing and unboxing?
cards.h: Boxing = putting a coin in a gift box.
s: Boxing is when a value type, like an int, is wrapped into an object on the heap, for example when you put it into an object variable or an old non-generic collection. Unboxing is getting the value back with a cast. It costs memory and time, so in hot code I avoid it by using generics, like List of int instead of ArrayList.
cards.k: boxing, unboxing, value types, performance, generics

cards.q: What is IDisposable, the using statement and the using declaration?
cards.h: using = auto-close the tap.
s: IDisposable is for objects that hold resources the garbage collector doesn't manage, like files, database connections or streams, and its Dispose method releases them. The using statement calls Dispose automatically at the end of the block, even if there's an exception. The newer using declaration does the same at the end of the current scope, with less nesting.

cards.q: const vs readonly vs static readonly?
cards.h: const = carved in stone; readonly = set at birth.
s: A const is fixed at compile time and copied into any code that uses it, so it's only for values that never change, like pi. A readonly field is set once, in the declaration or constructor, and can differ per object. A static readonly is set once for the whole class at runtime. I use static readonly for things like configuration defaults, because changing a const needs every caller recompiled.

cards.h: Single = there can be only one.

cards.q: Any() vs Count()?
cards.h: Any = is anybody home? Count = take a census.

cards.q: What happens if an exception occurs inside an async method?
cards.h: The error waits inside the Task until you await it.
s: The exception doesn't crash immediately, it's stored inside the returned Task. When I await the task, the exception is thrown again at that point, so normal try-catch works around the await. If nobody awaits the task, the exception can be lost. And with async void, it can crash the process, so I only use async void for event handlers.

cards.q: What is Dependency Injection and why do we use it?
cards.h: Don't build your tools; get them handed to you.
s: Dependency injection means a class receives the objects it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself. ASP.NET Core has a built-in container that creates and injects them. It makes code loosely coupled and easy to test, because in tests I can pass mocks. For example, our vendor exchange service gets its SFTP client factory and logger injected.
cards.k: dependency injection, di, ioc, constructor injection, loose coupling, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: What is a dependency?
cards.h: What you cannot work without.
s: A dependency is anything a class needs to do its job, like a repository, an HTTP client, a logger, configuration or even the current time. If a class creates these itself, it's tightly tied to them and hard to test. With dependency injection, they're passed in, so I can swap them, for example a fake time provider in tests.
cards.k: dependency, di, coupling

cards.q: What is Inversion of Control, and what is an IoC container?
cards.h: The container is the factory manager.
s: Inversion of control means the framework controls the flow and calls my code, instead of my code controlling everything. ASP.NET Core calls my middleware, controllers and services. An IoC container is the part that creates objects, injects their dependencies, and manages their lifetimes and disposal. The built-in .NET container does this for us.
cards.k: inversion of control, ioc, ioc container, di, dependency injection, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: Constructor injection vs property injection?
cards.h: Constructor = must-haves; property = nice-to-haves.
s: Constructor injection passes dependencies through the constructor, so required dependencies are obvious and the object is always fully ready. Property injection sets them through public properties after creation, which hides what's required and allows half-ready objects. The built-in .NET container supports constructor injection, and that's what I always use.
cards.k: constructor injection, property injection, di

cards.q: What is IServiceProvider?
cards.h: The vending machine for services.
s: IServiceProvider is the interface of the built-in DI container. It's what actually resolves services, using GetService or GetRequiredService. The root provider is created when the app is built, and each request gets its own scoped provider. In normal code I don't use it directly, I just use constructor injection. I use it mainly in factories or when creating scopes.
cards.k: iserviceprovider, di container, getservice, resolve

cards.q: Which lifetimes can depend on which (Singleton, Scoped, Transient)?
cards.h: Depend only on things that live at least as long as you.
s: The rule is that a service should only depend on services that live as long or longer. A singleton can depend only on singletons. A scoped service can depend on scoped and singleton services. A transient can depend on anything. A singleton depending on a scoped service, like DbContext, is a captive dependency bug, and ASP.NET Core catches it in development with scope validation.
cards.k: di lifetimes, captive dependency, singleton, scoped, transient

cards.q: GetService() vs GetRequiredService()?
cards.h: Required = fail loudly.
s: GetService returns null if the service isn't registered, so it's for optional services. GetRequiredService throws a clear exception naming the missing type, so it's for services that must exist. I prefer GetRequiredService, because a clear error at startup is much easier to fix than a NullReferenceException later.
cards.k: getservice, getrequiredservice, di, iserviceprovider

cards.q: How does constructor injection work in ASP.NET Core, and how are controller dependencies resolved?
cards.h: Per request: new scope, new controller, wired graph.
s: When a request comes in, ASP.NET Core creates the controller through the DI container. The container looks at the constructor, picks the one with the most parameters it can satisfy, resolves each dependency, and their dependencies, in the request scope. Scoped services are shared within that request. At the end of the request, the scope disposes them.
cards.k: constructor injection, controller dependencies, di, request scope

cards.q: How do you register and resolve multiple implementations of an interface?
cards.h: Many plugs: take the whole strip or ask by name.
s: I can register several implementations of the same interface, then inject IEnumerable of that interface to get all of them, in registration order, which is good for things like a list of validators. If I need one specific implementation, I use keyed services from .NET 8 with the FromKeyedServices attribute, or a small factory. We use keyed services to pick an SFTP library per vendor.
cards.k: multiple implementations, keyed services, ienumerable, di

cards.q: Can you manually create a scope, and when would you use IServiceScopeFactory?
cards.h: Open a meeting room when you need one.
s: Yes. I inject IServiceScopeFactory and call CreateScope, then resolve services from that scope and dispose it when done. I use it in singletons like background services, where there's no request scope, but I need scoped services like DbContext. For example, our SFTP poller creates a new scope for each polling run.
cards.k: iservicescopefactory, createscope, background service, scoped

cards.q: What is the service locator anti-pattern?
cards.h: Hidden dependencies are surprise bills.
s: The service locator anti-pattern is when a class asks the container for its dependencies itself, by injecting IServiceProvider and calling GetService everywhere. It hides the real dependencies, so you can't see them in the constructor, and tests become harder. It's fine in factories or framework code, but in business classes I always use constructor injection.
cards.k: service locator, anti-pattern, di, iserviceprovider

cards.q: How would you unit test a DI-based service?
cards.h: Unit tests use new, not the container.
s: Because dependencies come through the constructor, I just create the class in the test and pass mocks or fakes, for example a mocked ISftpClient with Moq and a fake time provider. Then I test the behaviour, like which file was uploaded or which error was returned. For bigger tests, I use WebApplicationFactory and replace only the external services.
cards.k: unit testing, di, mocking, moq, testing, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes, test, unit test, integration test, xunit, mock

cards.q: Give a real DI example from your application.
cards.h: Factory picks the plug; DI hands it over.
s: Our vendor exchange service gets an SFTP client factory, its settings through IOptions, and a logger, all through the constructor. The factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro client based on each vendor's configuration. The service is scoped, the factory is a singleton, and the clients are created and disposed for each transfer.
cards.k: di example, real example, sftp, story, di, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes

cards.q: Why shouldn't everything be Singleton, or everything Transient?
cards.h: Right lifetime for the right job.
s: Not everything should be singleton, because one shared instance must be thread-safe and must never hold per-request data, and it can't use scoped things like DbContext. Not everything should be transient either, because creating objects over and over wastes memory, and disposable transients can pile up. So I choose: singleton for stateless shared things, scoped for per-request, transient for light helpers.
cards.k: di lifetimes, singleton, transient, scoped, choosing lifetime

cards.q: What happens when a request ends?
cards.h: Meeting over: lights off, room cleaned.
s: When a request ends, the response is completed, and the request's DI scope is disposed, which disposes all scoped and transient services created in it, like DbContext, closing connections. If the client disconnected early, the request's cancellation token was already triggered, so well-written code stops work sooner. Then the HttpContext is released.
cards.k: request end, dispose, scope, request lifecycle

cards.q: Who disposes Scoped and Singleton services, and how does DI handle IDisposable dependencies?
cards.h: Whoever creates it, cleans it.
s: The container disposes what it creates. Scoped services, and transients resolved in a scope, are disposed when the scope ends, usually at the end of the request. Singletons are disposed when the application shuts down. If I create an object myself and register the instance, the container won't dispose it, so I must. And disposable transients resolved from the root stay alive until shutdown, which is a leak.
cards.k: dispose, idisposable, di, scoped, singleton, dependency injection, ioc, inversion of control, service container, service lifetime, lifetimes, garbage collection, gc, memory

cards.q: What is ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Modern .NET for the web, anywhere.
s: ASP.NET Core is Microsoft's modern, open-source and cross-platform framework for building web APIs, websites and real-time apps. It has built-in dependency injection, a middleware pipeline, configuration and logging, and it's one of the fastest web frameworks. It runs on Windows, Linux and in containers. All our IRT APIs are built on it.
cards.k: asp.net core, web framework, .net

cards.q: What is Kestrel?
cards.h: Kestrel = the engine inside every ASP.NET Core app.
s: Kestrel is the built-in, cross-platform web server in ASP.NET Core. It's very fast and supports HTTP 1, 2 and 3. It can face the internet directly, but often sits behind a reverse proxy or load balancer like an ALB, Nginx or IIS, which handles TLS and routing. Our containers run Kestrel behind an ALB.
cards.k: kestrel, web server, reverse proxy, asp.net core

cards.q: What happens if middleware is registered in the wrong order?
cards.h: Wrong order = guard checks tickets before checking ID.
s: Middleware runs in the order it's added, so wrong order causes real bugs. For example, if authorization is added before authentication, the user isn't known yet and every request fails. If the exception handler is added late, earlier errors aren't caught. And if CORS is added after the endpoints, preflight requests don't get the right headers and the browser blocks the call.
cards.k: middleware order, pipeline order, bugs, cors, authentication, middleware, pipeline, request delegate, request pipeline

cards.q: Use vs Run vs Map?
cards.h: Use = pass along, Run = stop here, Map = fork.
s: Use adds middleware that can do work and then call the next one. Run adds terminal middleware that ends the pipeline, so nothing after it runs. Map branches the pipeline based on the path, so requests to, say, /health go down a separate pipeline. For normal routes I use endpoint routing like MapGet or MapControllers.
cards.k: use, run, map, middleware, pipeline branching

cards.q: What is endpoint routing?
cards.h: Pick the destination first, check the ticket, then travel.
s: With endpoint routing, the routing middleware matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on the HttpContext. So middleware in between, like CORS, authentication, authorization and rate limiting, can read the endpoint's metadata, such as the Authorize attribute or a rate limit policy. Then the endpoint itself runs at the end.
cards.k: endpoint routing, userouting, endpoints, metadata

cards.q: What happened to Startup.cs?
cards.h: Two files became one.
s: Since .NET 6, the separate Startup class and Program class were merged into one Program.cs using the minimal hosting model. Service registrations that were in ConfigureServices go on builder.Services, and the pipeline that was in Configure goes on the app object. Startup still works if you want it, but new projects don't use it.
cards.k: startup.cs, program.cs, minimal hosting, .net 6

cards.q: Does CORS provide security?
cards.h: CORS is a browser courtesy, not a lock.
s: No, CORS is not a security feature for the API. It's a browser rule that relaxes the same-origin policy, telling the browser which other sites may read responses. Tools like Postman or a server can call the API regardless of CORS. So real security still comes from authentication and authorization. CORS only protects users in the browser.
cards.k: cors, security, same-origin policy, browser, owasp, xss, csrf, sql injection, cookie

cards.q: How do you configure HTTPS?
cards.h: Encrypt every hop that matters.
s: In development I use the dev certificate. In production, HTTPS is usually terminated at the load balancer, like our ALB, with a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager. In the app I add UseHttpsRedirection and HSTS, and configure forwarded headers so the app knows the original request was HTTPS. Traffic between services is also encrypted.
cards.k: https, tls, certificates, hsts, ssl

cards.q: What is health checking?
cards.h: A pulse and a ready sign.
s: Health checks are endpoints that report if the app and its dependencies are healthy. In ASP.NET Core I add AddHealthChecks with checks for things like the database and the message broker, and map them to endpoints. I keep a simple liveness endpoint and a readiness endpoint that checks dependencies. The load balancer and ECS use them to route traffic only to healthy instances.
cards.k: health checks, liveness, readiness, monitoring, load balancer

cards.q: How do you implement graceful shutdown?
cards.h: Finish the plates on the table, take no new orders.
s: When a container is stopped, it gets a SIGTERM signal. ASP.NET Core stops accepting new requests, lets current ones finish within the shutdown timeout, which is 30 seconds by default, and cancels the stopping token for background services. I make my background loops respect that token and finish or save their work. The load balancer also drains connections first.
cards.k: graceful shutdown, sigterm, shutdown timeout, stopping token

cards.q: How do you handle cancellation tokens?
cards.h: If the caller hangs up, stop cooking.
s: I accept a CancellationToken in my async methods and pass it all the way down, to EF Core queries and HTTP calls. In APIs, ASP.NET Core gives a token that's cancelled if the client disconnects, so we stop wasting work. In background services I use the stopping token. I never ignore it, and I treat a cancellation exception as normal, not an error.
cards.k: cancellation token, cancellation, async, requestaborted

cards.q: PUT vs PATCH?
cards.h: PUT = replace the form; PATCH = correct one box.
s: PUT replaces the whole resource with what I send, so missing fields can be cleared, and it's idempotent. PATCH updates only the fields I send, which is better for small changes. For PATCH, I use JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch. In our APIs, we use PATCH for things like updating only a shipment's status.
cards.k: put, patch, http verbs, rest, partial update

cards.h: 201 = born.
s: 200 OK means the request succeeded and the result is in the body. 201 Created means a new resource was created, and the response should include a Location header pointing to it, usually with the created item. So for a POST that creates a shipment, I return 201 with the link to the new shipment.
cards.k: 200, 201, status codes, created, rest

cards.h: 400 = bad form, 401 = who are you, 403 = not you.
s: 400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong, like invalid JSON or failed validation. 401 Unauthorized actually means not authenticated: no token, or an invalid or expired one. 403 Forbidden means we know who you are, but you're not allowed to do this. So a logged-in user trying to open another study's data gets 403.
cards.k: 400, 401, 403, status codes, unauthorized, forbidden

cards.h: 404 = wrong address; 405 = right address, wrong door.
s: 404 Not Found means the resource or route doesn't exist, like asking for a shipment id that isn't there. 405 Method Not Allowed means the route exists, but not for that HTTP method, like sending DELETE to an endpoint that only supports GET. ASP.NET Core returns 405 automatically in that case.
cards.k: 404, 405, status codes, not found, method not allowed

cards.h: 409 = clash with reality; 422 = makes no sense.
s: 409 Conflict means the request conflicts with the current state, like creating a site number that already exists, or a concurrency conflict when someone else changed the record. 422 means the request is well-formed but breaks a business rule, like asking for more kits than the depot has. Both tell the client exactly what kind of problem to fix.
cards.k: 409, 422, status codes, conflict, validation

cards.h: 500 = I broke, 502 = my supplier broke, 503 = closed for now.
s: 500 means something broke inside our service. 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer got an invalid response from the service behind it, for example the container crashed. 503 Service Unavailable means the service is temporarily overloaded or in maintenance, ideally with a Retry-After header. When I troubleshoot, these tell me which layer to look at first.
cards.k: 500, 502, 503, status codes, server error

cards.q: What are DTOs and why use them?
cards.h: DTO = the envelope, not the whole filing cabinet.
s: A DTO, or data transfer object, is a simple class that defines exactly what the API sends or receives. It keeps the API contract separate from the database entities. So I can change the database without breaking clients, avoid exposing sensitive fields, and prevent over-posting. I use C# records for DTOs.
cards.k: dto, data transfer object, api contract, records

cards.q: Why shouldn't you expose EF entities directly?
cards.h: Show the menu, not the kitchen.
s: Returning EF entities directly ties the API to the database design, so a schema change breaks clients. It can also leak sensitive or internal fields, create circular references when serializing, trigger lazy loading, and allow over-posting on input. In a clinical system, accidentally exposing an unblinding field would be serious, so we always map to DTOs.
cards.k: ef entities, dto, security, over-posting, api design

cards.q: DTO vs ViewModel?
cards.h: DTO travels; ViewModel is displayed.
s: A DTO carries data across a boundary, like an API request or response, and has no behaviour. A ViewModel is shaped for a specific screen in server-rendered MVC or Razor pages, and can include display-specific data. With a React front end, our APIs return DTOs, and the client shapes its own view state.
cards.k: dto, viewmodel, mvc, api

cards.q: What is [ApiController]?
cards.h: One attribute, API manners included.
s: The ApiController attribute turns on API-friendly behaviours: it automatically returns a 400 with validation errors when the model is invalid, infers where parameters come from, like body or route, requires attribute routing, and returns errors as ProblemDetails. It removes a lot of repetitive code from every action.
cards.k: apicontroller, attribute, model validation, problemdetails

cards.q: What is routing, and attribute routing vs conventional routing?
cards.h: Attribute = address on each door; conventional = one street map.
s: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to the code that handles it. Attribute routing puts the route on the controller or action, like Route api slash shipments, which is clear and flexible, and it's the standard for APIs. Conventional routing uses one central pattern, like controller slash action slash id, which is common in older MVC apps.
cards.k: routing, attribute routing, conventional routing, endpoints

cards.q: How do you implement filtering and sorting?
cards.h: Filter, sort, then page, all in SQL.
s: I accept filter and sort parameters in the query string, but only for a known list of fields, never raw SQL or any column name. I build the query step by step on IQueryable, adding Where clauses for each filter and an OrderBy for the sort, then apply paging. Everything runs in the database, and the most used filters have indexes.
cards.k: filtering, sorting, paging, iqueryable, query parameters

cards.q: How do you document APIs, and what is Swagger/OpenAPI?
cards.h: OpenAPI = the API's manual.
s: OpenAPI is a standard way to describe an API: endpoints, parameters, request and response models and status codes. Swagger is the tooling around it, like the interactive Swagger UI. In .NET, I generate the document from the code, and since .NET 9 it's built in. We share it with front-end and vendor teams and generate clients from it.
cards.k: swagger, openapi, api documentation, swagger ui

cards.q: How do you secure an API?
cards.h: Lock, ID check, permission, limits, logs.
s: I secure an API in layers: HTTPS everywhere, authentication with JWT from our identity provider, authorization with policies and per-record checks, input validation, and DTOs so we don't leak data. Then rate limiting, secure headers, secrets in Secrets Manager, logging without sensitive data, and regular dependency and security scans.
cards.k: api security, authentication, authorization, jwt, owasp, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Access token vs refresh token?
cards.h: Access = day pass; refresh = membership card at reception.
s: An access token is short-lived, maybe [15 minutes], and is sent with every API call to prove who you are. A refresh token lives longer and is used only to get a new access token from the identity provider, without logging in again. If an access token leaks, it expires soon, and refresh tokens can be revoked. That's how we fixed our logout issue.
cards.k: access token, refresh token, jwt, oauth, token lifetime, token, bearer

cards.q: Role-based vs policy-based authorization, and how do you implement policies?
cards.h: Roles = job title; policies = specific rules.
s: Role-based authorization checks if the user is in a role, like Admin. Policy-based authorization is more flexible: a policy is a set of requirements, like a claim, a role, or custom logic, written in a handler. I register policies with AddAuthorization, then use them on endpoints. We use policies for things like checking the user has access to a specific study.
cards.k: role-based authorization, policy-based authorization, policies, authorization handler

cards.q: How do you prevent over-posting?
cards.h: Only accept what is on the form.
s: Over-posting is when a client sends extra fields, like isAdmin, and the server saves them because it binds directly to the entity. I prevent it by binding only to request DTOs that contain just the allowed fields, then mapping them to entities myself. I also have tests that send extra fields and check they're ignored.
cards.k: over-posting, mass assignment, dto, security

cards.q: How do you handle large request payloads?
cards.h: Big things go by freight, not in the envelope.
s: First I set sensible size limits, in Kestrel and per endpoint, so huge requests are rejected early. For large data, I don't buffer everything in memory, I stream the request body. For really large files, the client uploads directly to S3 with a presigned URL, and the API only receives a reference. For big imports, I process them in the background.
cards.k: large payloads, request size limit, streaming, s3, upload

cards.q: How do you handle file uploads?
cards.h: Check it, store it safely, process it later.
s: For small files, I accept IFormFile with a size limit, check the extension and the actual content, and never trust the file name. I store files outside the web root, like S3, and scan them if needed. For large files, I use presigned S3 uploads or stream the multipart body. Our CSV import checks size, format and content before processing.
cards.k: file upload, iformfile, multipart, s3, validation

cards.q: How do you design a production-ready API?
cards.h: Contract, Security, Resilience, Observability, Performance.
s: A production-ready API needs clear contracts with DTOs and OpenAPI, validation and consistent ProblemDetails errors, and security with authentication, authorization and rate limits. It needs logging with correlation ids, metrics and health checks, resilience with timeouts and retries, and paging for lists. Plus startup checks for configuration, versioning, and automated tests in the pipeline.
cards.k: production ready api, api design, best practices, checklist, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Where should validation happen?
cards.h: Door, desk, and vault each check.
s: Validation happens at several layers, each with its own job. The API checks the shape and format of the request. The service layer checks business rules, like a site must belong to an active depot. The database enforces constraints, like unique site numbers, as the final safety net. That way bad data is stopped as early as possible, but nothing slips through.
cards.k: validation, layers, business rules, constraints

cards.q: How do you prevent duplicate requests?
cards.h: Same key, same answer, done once.
s: For requests that create something, I use an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key, and the server stores it with the result, so a repeated request returns the same result instead of creating a duplicate. I also add unique constraints in the database. Our CSV import uses a file hash to block importing the same file twice.
cards.k: duplicate requests, idempotency key, idempotency, unique constraint

cards.q: What is Entity Framework Core?
cards.h: Objects in, SQL out.
s: Entity Framework Core is Microsoft's ORM for .NET. It lets me work with the database using C# classes and LINQ, and it translates my queries into SQL, tracks changes to objects, and saves them back. It also handles migrations for schema changes. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL and others. Most of our IRT services use EF Core with SQL Server.
cards.k: ef core, entity framework, orm, database, ef, dbcontext, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: EF Core vs ADO.NET?
cards.h: ADO.NET = manual gearbox; EF Core = automatic.
s: ADO.NET is the low-level way: I open connections, write SQL, and read rows manually, which gives full control and top speed but more code. EF Core sits on top of ADO.NET and does the mapping, change tracking and SQL generation for me, so I'm much more productive. I use EF Core by default, and Dapper or raw SQL for a few performance-critical or reporting queries.
cards.k: ef core, ado.net, dapper, orm, comparison, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is DbContext, and what is DbSet?
cards.h: DbContext = the session; DbSet = a table inside it.
s: DbContext is the main EF Core class. It represents a session with the database: it manages the connection, tracks changes, and saves them in a transaction. A DbSet is a property on the DbContext for one entity type, like Shipments, which I query with LINQ and add or remove from. DbContext is short-lived, one per request.
cards.k: dbcontext, dbset, ef core, entity framework, ef, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: Include() vs ThenInclude()?
cards.h: Include = children; ThenInclude = grandchildren.
s: Include loads a related entity together with the main one, like shipments with their site. ThenInclude goes one level deeper from that related entity, like the site's country. Both turn into joins in a single query. I use them carefully, because including too much can load a lot of data. For read screens, I often use a Select projection instead.
cards.k: include, theninclude, eager loading, ef core

cards.q: How do you create EF migrations?
cards.h: Add, review, script, release.
s: I change my entity classes or configuration, then run dotnet ef migrations add with a clear name. EF Core compares the model with the last snapshot and generates a migration with Up and Down methods. I review the generated code. For deployment, we generate an idempotent SQL script, review it, and apply it as a controlled step in the release, not automatically at startup.
cards.k: ef core migrations, dotnet ef, schema changes, database

cards.q: Code First vs Database First?
cards.h: Code drives DB, or DB drives code.
s: Code First means I write the C# entity classes first and EF Core creates and updates the database with migrations. Database First means the database already exists and I generate the classes from it with scaffolding. For new services I use Code First, and for an existing database I scaffold once and can then continue with Code First.
cards.k: code first, database first, scaffolding, ef core

cards.q: What is LINQ-to-Entities?
cards.h: LINQ that speaks SQL.
s: LINQ to Entities is LINQ used against EF Core. Instead of running in memory, my LINQ query becomes an expression tree that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database. So Where, Select and OrderBy happen in SQL Server. I can see the generated SQL with ToQueryString, which helps when tuning.
cards.k: linq to entities, ef core, iqueryable, sql translation, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq, ienumerable, deferred execution

cards.q: What causes client-side evaluation?
cards.h: If SQL can't say it, EF won't run it in the DB.
s: Client-side evaluation happens when part of a query can't be translated into SQL, like calling my own C# method inside a Where. Since EF Core 3, that throws an error instead of quietly loading all rows into memory, which was a big performance trap. Only the final Select can run in C#. I fix it by rewriting the query with translatable expressions.
cards.k: client-side evaluation, ef core, query translation, performance

cards.q: How do you optimize EF Core queries and performance?
cards.h: Track less, select less, round-trip less.
s: First I look at the generated SQL and the execution plan. Then the usual fixes: use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, project only the columns I need with Select, avoid N+1 queries, add paging, and make sure the right indexes exist. For big updates I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. That's how our shipment list went from [9 seconds to under 300 milliseconds].
cards.k: ef core performance, optimization, asnotracking, projection, n+1, ef core, entity framework, ef, dbcontext, orm, migrations, linq to entities

cards.q: What is SaveChanges(), and SaveChanges() vs SaveChangesAsync()?
cards.h: One commit for all changes; async frees the thread.
s: SaveChanges looks at all the tracked changes and writes them to the database as inserts, updates and deletes, inside one transaction by default. SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking the thread while waiting for the database. In ASP.NET Core I always use SaveChangesAsync, so the server can handle other requests meanwhile.
cards.k: savechanges, savechangesasync, ef core, transactions

cards.q: How do you handle bulk operations?
cards.h: Bulk = set-based, not row by row.
s: For large updates or deletes, I use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which run one SQL statement without loading entities into memory. For large inserts, I batch them, or use SqlBulkCopy or a bulk extension library, which is much faster than adding thousands of entities one by one. Our CSV import saves rows in batches inside one transaction.
cards.k: bulk operations, executeupdate, executedelete, sqlbulkcopy, ef core

cards.q: What are compiled queries?
cards.h: Translate once, run many.
s: A compiled query is a LINQ query that EF Core translates once and then reuses, using EF.CompileAsyncQuery. EF Core already caches query plans, so this only saves the small cost of processing the query each time. I'd use it only for very hot queries that run thousands of times per second, after measuring.

cards.q: How do you log generated SQL?
cards.h: See the SQL before you trust it.
s: I set the log level for the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command category to Information, and EF Core logs every SQL command it runs, with timings. For a single query, ToQueryString shows the SQL without running it. I never turn on sensitive data logging in production, because it would log parameter values.

cards.q: How do you handle relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many?
cards.h: 1:1 pair, 1:N parent, N:N join table.
s: In EF Core, I define relationships with navigation properties and configure them with the Fluent API. One-to-many is the most common, like a site with many shipments, using a foreign key on the shipment. One-to-one uses a foreign key with a unique constraint. Many-to-many can be automatic with a hidden join table, or an explicit join entity if it needs extra columns.

cards.q: What are shadow properties?
cards.h: Columns the class never sees.
s: A shadow property is a column that EF Core knows about but that isn't a property on my C# class. I access it through the change tracker or EF.Property. It's handy for things like audit columns, such as created date or updated by, which I set in SaveChanges without cluttering my domain classes.

cards.q: What is owned entity mapping?
cards.h: Owned = lives inside its owner.
s: An owned entity is a type that has no identity of its own and belongs to its owner, like an Address inside a Site. By default its columns are stored in the owner's table, with prefixed names. It's a nice way to model value objects. In EF Core 8 there are also complex types for the same idea.

cards.q: How do you configure indexes in EF Core?
cards.h: Index in code, built by migration.
s: I configure indexes in OnModelCreating with HasIndex, or with the Index attribute on the class. I can make them unique, combine several columns, add a filter, and include extra columns for SQL Server. Then a migration creates them. For example, a unique index on study and site number stops duplicate sites.
