cards.q: Design a scalable REST API or a high-volume API.
cards.h: Stateless, cached, paged, async, limited.
s: I'd keep the API stateless behind a load balancer so I can add instances, with autoscaling. I'd add caching for hot reads, pagination for lists, async processing for heavy work, and rate limits. For the database, indexes first, then read replicas, and partitioning if needed. And I'd monitor p95 latency and errors.
cards.k: scalable api, high volume, system design, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Design a URL shortener.
cards.h: Encode an id, cache the hot ones, redirect fast.
s: The service takes a long URL and returns a short code, like a base62 version of a unique id, and stores the mapping in a database. When someone opens the short link, it looks up the code and redirects, using a cache like Redis for popular links. I'd add expiry, abuse protection, and click analytics if needed.
cards.k: url shortener, system design, base62, redis

cards.q: Design a notification service.
cards.h: Event in, preferences, template, channel workers.
s: Other services publish a notification request to a queue. Workers for each channel, like email, SMS and push, pick it up, apply templates and the user's preferences, and send through providers. Failed sends are retried with backoff and then go to a dead-letter queue. An idempotency key prevents duplicate messages.
cards.k: notification service, system design, queues, email, sms

cards.q: Design an order management system.
cards.h: Saga over services, state machine per order.
s: I'd model the order as a state machine with clear allowed transitions, like created, paid, shipped and delivered. Placing an order reserves stock and takes payment through a saga, with compensating actions if a step fails. Events are published through an outbox, and APIs use idempotency keys so retries don't create duplicate orders.
cards.k: order management, system design, saga, state machine

cards.q: Design a file upload service.
cards.h: Presigned upload, scan on arrival.
s: The client asks the API for a presigned S3 URL and uploads directly to S3, so large files don't go through our servers. An S3 event then triggers processing, like virus scanning and extracting metadata. I'd use multipart upload for big files, size limits, and store file details in a database with access control.
cards.k: file upload service, system design, s3, presigned url

cards.q: Design a distributed job-processing system.
cards.h: Enqueue, work, retry, dead-letter, report.
s: Jobs go into a queue, and a pool of workers picks them up. Each job is idempotent, so retries are safe, failed jobs are retried with backoff and then sent to a dead-letter queue. I track each job's status in a database so users can see progress, and scale the workers based on the queue length.
cards.k: job processing, distributed jobs, workers, queues, system design

cards.q: Design a payment system.
cards.h: Idempotent, double-entry, reconciled.
s: Every payment request carries an idempotency key, so a retry never charges twice. I'd keep a ledger with double-entry records and reconcile it with the payment provider daily. Card data is never stored by us, we use a PCI-compliant provider with tokens. Payment status updates come through provider webhooks.
cards.k: payment system, system design, idempotency, ledger

cards.q: Design a messaging (chat) system.
cards.h: Sockets in, persist, fan out.
s: Clients connect with WebSockets, using SignalR in .NET, for live messages. Messages are stored per conversation with an ordering id, and delivered to online users instantly, while offline users get a push notification and fetch messages later. To scale across servers, I'd use a backplane like Redis.
cards.k: chat system, messaging, system design, websockets, signalr, message broker, kafka, rabbitmq, event driven

cards.q: Design an event-driven microservices system.
cards.h: Outbox, broker, idempotent consumers.
s: Services publish events when something important happens, and other services react to them. Events are versioned contracts with schemas, published reliably through an outbox, and consumers are idempotent. For simple flows, services react on their own, and for longer business processes, an orchestrator saga gives better visibility.
cards.k: event-driven, microservices, system design, events, outbox, messaging, message broker, kafka, rabbitmq, event driven, microservice, service boundary, bounded context, distributed

cards.q: Design a scalable authentication system.
cards.h: Central IdP, stateless tokens, fast local validation.
s: I wouldn't build my own, I'd use a proven identity provider with OpenID Connect. Apps use short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation, and MFA for users. For logout or revocation, a denylist of token ids in Redis works, like our fix with [15-minute] tokens and about [1 millisecond] checks.
cards.k: authentication system, system design, oidc, tokens

cards.q: Design a distributed caching system.
cards.h: Hash ring, TTL, invalidate, avoid stampedes.
s: I'd use cache-aside with expiry times, spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing, and invalidate entries when data changes. To avoid a stampede, where many requests rebuild the same entry at once, I'd use request coalescing, which HybridCache in .NET does for us. Redis cluster is the usual choice.
cards.k: distributed cache, caching, redis, system design

cards.q: Design your IQVIA-style clinical-trial platform at a high level.
cards.h: Setup, Randomize, Supply, Ship, Audit.
s: Users and vendors come in through a gateway with SSO. Behind it are services for study setup, randomization, supply, shipments and subjects, each with its own SQL Server database and audit tables. Kafka and RabbitMQ carry events and work queues, vendor integrations use SFTP and APIs, everything runs on ECS across availability zones, and GxP controls like validation and audit trails apply throughout.
cards.k: clinical trial platform, irt design, system design, architecture

cards.q: How would you scale the architecture, and handle database scaling?
cards.h: Scale out the services, tune then split the data.
s: I'd scale services horizontally since they're stateless, cache reference data, and move heavy work to queues. For the database, first tune queries and indexes, then add read replicas for reporting, and finally partition data, for example by study, if one database can't keep up.
cards.k: scaling, database scaling, read replicas, partitioning

cards.q: Where would you use caching, Kafka, RabbitMQ and synchronous APIs?
cards.h: Cache what's read, Kafka what's streamed, Rabbit what's queued, REST what's asked.
s: I'd use caching for reference data and permissions, in Redis. Kafka for shipment status events that many services consume and we may need to replay. RabbitMQ for task-style work like notifications and reports, with retries per message. And synchronous APIs for user-facing reads and commands that need an immediate answer, like randomizing a patient.
cards.k: caching, kafka, rabbitmq, synchronous apis, design choices, topic, partition, consumer group, offset, event streaming, queue, exchange, amqp, dead letter, dlq, messaging, message broker, event driven

cards.q: How would you handle failures?
cards.h: Expect failure everywhere.
s: I'd use timeouts on every call, retries with backoff for temporary errors, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues and the outbox pattern so nothing is lost. Each failure is visible through alerts, with runbooks so the on-call person knows what to do.
cards.k: failure handling, resilience, outbox, dlq

cards.q: How would you monitor and secure the system?
cards.h: Watch everything; trust nothing.
s: To monitor, I'd use metrics, logs and traces with correlation ids, and alerts based on service level objectives. To secure it, SSO for users, role-based access, encryption everywhere, audit trails for all regulated data, and least-privilege IAM roles for the services.
cards.k: monitoring, security, observability, system design

cards.q: Did you process the CSV import synchronously or asynchronously?
cards.h: Small capped file: answer now; big file: job and poll.
s: I processed it synchronously within the request, because files are limited to [5 MB, about 10,000 rows], and parsing is streamed, so validation finishes in [a few seconds] and users see the preview right away. All the file and database work is async, so no threads are blocked. For much bigger files, I'd move it to a background job that returns 202 with a status endpoint.
cards.k: csv import, synchronous, asynchronous, background job, 202

cards.q: How did you secure uploaded files?
cards.h: Who, how big, what type, never executed.
s: Only authorised users with the right role for that study can upload. I check the size limit, the CSV extension, and that the content really is text CSV. Files are processed in memory or temporary storage, never executed or served back. When we export the error report, I protect against CSV injection, and every upload is audited with who uploaded what.
cards.k: file upload security, csv injection, validation, audit

cards.q: How did you optimize large CSV processing?
cards.h: Stream, preload lookups, batch writes.
s: I read the file as a stream with CsvHelper instead of loading it all into memory. Validation runs in stages and stops early if the headers are wrong. Lookups, like existing sites, countries and depots, are loaded once into dictionaries, instead of a database call per row. Then rows are inserted in batches inside one transaction.
cards.k: csv performance, streaming, csvhelper, batching, optimization

cards.q: How did you test the import?
cards.h: Every rule, the whole save, the real UI.
s: I wrote unit tests for each validation rule, like missing fields, wrong types, duplicates in the file or database, and invalid countries or depots. Integration tests saved a file into a test database and checked that a failure rolls everything back. Playwright tests covered upload, preview, error download and confirm. I also tested a file at the maximum size.
cards.k: csv import testing, unit tests, integration tests, playwright, test, testing, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How did you handle concurrent imports?
cards.h: One study, one import at a time.
s: Only one import per study can run at a time, enforced by a lock row checked inside the transaction, so a second user gets a clear "import in progress" message. A file hash stops the same file being imported twice. And a [limit of 2 imports per user] at a time protects the server.
cards.k: concurrent imports, locking, concurrency, file hash

cards.q: What happens if the import fails halfway through?
cards.h: All or nothing means halfway = nothing.
s: Nothing is saved. All rows are written in one transaction, so if anything fails, like a database error or timeout, everything is rolled back. The user sees a clear error and can simply try again, and the audit log records the failed attempt. The study is never left half set up.
cards.k: import failure, transaction, rollback, atomicity

cards.q: How would you redesign it for millions of records?
cards.h: S3, worker, staging table, bulk copy, merge.
s: For millions of rows, I'd upload directly to S3 with a presigned URL. A background worker would stream and validate the file in chunks, load rows into a staging table with SqlBulkCopy, validate them with set-based SQL, and then merge them into the live tables in controlled batches, with progress reporting and an error file. A file hash and job id keep it idempotent.
cards.k: large scale import, millions of records, sqlbulkcopy, staging table, s3

cards.q: How did you test the study transfer safety guard?
cards.h: Each rule pass and fail, plus the race.
s: I wrote unit tests for each of the five checks, both passing and failing, like a live study with randomized patients or a missing change request. Integration tests covered the transaction and the lock, including two transfers at once. Tests confirmed every attempt is audited, and the FV scripts cover each blocking scenario.
cards.k: testing, study transfer, safety guard, unit tests, test, unit test, integration test, xunit, moq, mock

cards.q: How did you audit blocked transfers?
cards.h: Blocked attempts are evidence, not noise.
s: Every attempt, allowed or blocked, writes an audit record with the user, the source and target study and environment, the change request reference, which check failed and why, and the time. The audit is written separately, so it's saved even when the transfer is blocked. Validators and support can report on blocked attempts.
cards.k: audit, blocked transfers, audit trail, gxp

cards.q: What is release integration?
cards.h: Many teams in, one tagged release out.
s: Release integration means bringing together every team's changes for a release, the application, APIs, database scripts and UI, merging them into the release branch, resolving conflicts, tagging one version, and producing a consistent set of artifacts to install and validate. I'm the release integrator for our team, coordinating with about [5] teams.
cards.k: release integration, release management, merging, tagging

cards.q: How do you validate releases and promote from UAT to production?
cards.h: Same artifact, proven in UAT, approved for production.
s: We validate with automated tests, smoke tests after install, version checks on every node, FV scripts with evidence, and UAT sign-off. To promote to production, we take the exact same tagged artifacts that passed UAT, under an approved change request, deploy them through the controlled pipeline, and verify afterwards.
cards.k: release validation, uat to production, promotion, change request

cards.q: How do you coordinate application, API, database and UI releases?
cards.h: DB first, then API, then app, then UI.
s: We use one release version and one checklist. The deployment order is backward-compatible database scripts first, then APIs, then application services, then the UI. Incomplete features stay behind feature flags, and I do a daily status check with each team in the days before the release.
cards.k: release coordination, deployment order, feature flags, api, rest, web api, endpoint, http

cards.q: Why use Python and Shell automation?
cards.h: Scripts make every node identical.
s: Our nodes run Linux-based install steps, where Shell is natural. Python handles the logic, like reading manifests, comparing versions and calling APIs. Together with Ansible, they make installs repeatable and identical on every node, which removed a lot of manual steps and mistakes.
cards.k: python, shell, ansible, automation, scripting

cards.q: How do you perform multi-node deployments and ensure all nodes run the same version?
cards.h: Same playbook everywhere, then compare versions.
s: Ansible playbooks with Python and Shell scripts run the install steps across [4 to 6] nodes in order, and stop if something fails. Each node reports its installed version, through a version file and a health endpoint, and a check compares them with the release tag. Any mismatch fails the verification.
cards.k: multi-node deployment, version check, ansible, consistency

cards.q: How do you verify a deployment?
cards.h: Version, health, smoke, logs, sign-off.
s: I check the version on every node, make sure the health endpoints are green, and run smoke tests of key flows, like login, randomizing in a test study, and the shipment list. Then I check logs and dashboards for any new errors, and sign off in the release record.
cards.k: deployment verification, smoke tests, health checks

cards.q: What is Agile, and Scrum vs Kanban?
cards.h: Scrum = timeboxes; Kanban = flow.
s: Agile means delivering in small pieces, getting feedback often and adapting. Scrum uses fixed-length sprints with roles like product owner and scrum master, and events like planning, review and retrospective. Kanban uses a continuous flow with limits on work in progress and no sprints, which suits support and operations work. Our team uses Scrum with [two-week] sprints.
cards.k: agile, scrum, kanban, methodology

cards.q: What happens during sprint planning, and what is a retrospective?
cards.h: Plan what to do; reflect on how we did it.
s: In sprint planning, the team picks the top priority, refined stories that fit our capacity, agrees a sprint goal, and breaks stories into tasks. The retrospective happens at the end of the sprint, where we talk about what went well and what didn't, and agree one or two improvements to try next sprint.
cards.k: sprint planning, retrospective, scrum, agile

cards.q: How do you handle changing requirements?
cards.h: Welcome the change, trade the scope.
s: First I understand why it's changing and how important it is, by talking with the product owner and BA. Then I estimate the impact and we agree what moves out of the sprint, and we update the acceptance criteria and traceability, which matters in GxP. I also write code that's easy to change, with clean boundaries and tests.
cards.k: changing requirements, scope change, agile

cards.q: How do you conduct code reviews, and handle disagreement during review?
cards.h: Review the code, respect the coder.
s: I review for correctness, security, readability, tests and design, and I keep comments about the code, not the person, explaining why and marking what's a must-fix versus a suggestion. If we disagree, I bring data, like documentation or our team standards. If comments keep going back and forth, I have a quick call, and if needed, we agree a team rule with the lead.
cards.k: code review, disagreement, pull requests, feedback

cards.q: Tell me about a technical decision you influenced.

I addressed their safety concerns, like using each person's own token and keeping approvals, and measured before and after. The team adopted it: 6 hours to 2, and 6 people to 1.

cards.q: What is Spring Boot?
cards.h: Spring Boot = ASP.NET Core for Java.
s: Spring Boot is a framework on top of Spring for building Java services quickly. It gives auto-configuration, an embedded web server like Tomcat, starter dependencies, and production features like health and metrics with Actuator. It's basically the Java counterpart of ASP.NET Core.

cards.q: Dependency injection and the IoC container in Spring; @Autowired?
cards.h: Same DI idea, different annotations.
s: Spring's IoC container, the ApplicationContext, creates objects called beans and injects their dependencies, just like the .NET service provider. Constructor injection is the preferred way. The Autowired annotation marks where to inject, and if a class has only one constructor, it's not even needed.

cards.q: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository?
cards.h: Same bean, different labels; Repository also translates errors.
s: All three register a class as a Spring bean through component scanning. Component is the generic one. Service marks business logic, and it's mostly for readability. Repository marks data access classes and also translates database exceptions into Spring's standard data access exceptions.
cards.k: component, service, repository, spring annotations

cards.q: How do you build a Spring Boot REST controller?
cards.h: @RestController = [ApiController].
s: I create a class with the RestController annotation and a base path with RequestMapping, like api slash shipments. Methods use GetMapping and PostMapping. Parameters come from PathVariable, RequestParam, or RequestBody with Valid for validation. I return ResponseEntity to control the status code, just like returning results in ASP.NET Core.

cards.q: Spring Boot configuration and profiles?
cards.h: Profiles = appsettings.{Environment}.json.
s: Spring Boot reads configuration from application.yml or properties files, environment variables, and typed ConfigurationProperties classes, which are like the .NET options pattern. Profiles, like dev, uat and prod, load their own application-profile.yml file, and are chosen with spring.profiles.active, similar to ASP.NET Core environments.

cards.q: Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, and JPA vs EF Core?
cards.h: JPA = spec, Hibernate = engine, Spring Data = shortcuts.
s: JPA is the Java standard for persistence, Hibernate is the most common implementation, and Spring Data JPA adds repository interfaces that generate queries from method names. Compared with EF Core, the ideas are very similar, entities, change tracking and lazy loading. But migrations use Flyway or Liquibase, and queries use JPQL instead of LINQ.

cards.q: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core?
cards.h: Russian dolls: each layer wraps the next, in on the way in, out on the way back.
s: Middleware is a piece of code that sits in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. Every request passes through the middleware in the order I register them, and each one can do some work, call the next one, and then do more work on the way back, or stop the request early. Authentication, routing, CORS and exception handling are all middleware. In my project, I wrote a correlation-id middleware so we could trace every request across [4] services.

cards.q: What is custom middleware, and how do you write one?
cards.h: Before, next, after.
s: To write custom middleware, I create a class with a constructor that takes the next RequestDelegate and an InvokeAsync method that takes HttpContext. Inside, I do my work, await next, and then do any work after the response. Then I register it in Program.cs with app.UseMiddleware, at the right position. Our correlation-id middleware reads or creates an id, adds it to the response header and the logging scope, and then calls next.

cards.q: Convention-based vs factory-based (IMiddleware) middleware, and the scoped-service pitfall?
cards.h: Constructor = once forever; InvokeAsync parameters = per request.
s: Convention-based middleware is created once at startup, so it is effectively a singleton, and scoped services must be passed as parameters to InvokeAsync, not the constructor. Factory-based middleware implements IMiddleware and is created from DI for each request, so constructor injection of scoped services is fine, but I must register it in the container. The pitfall is injecting a scoped service like DbContext into a convention middleware's constructor, which captures it forever.

cards.q: What is IHttpClientFactory, and why not new HttpClient()?
cards.h: Factory = a pool of phone lines, refreshed regularly.
s: IHttpClientFactory creates HttpClient instances for me and manages the underlying connections. If I create new HttpClient for every call, sockets can run out, and if I keep one forever, it may miss DNS changes. The factory pools and recycles handlers to solve both. It also lets me configure typed clients with base address, headers and resilience policies in one place, which is how we call vendor and internal APIs.

cards.q: What are Span<T> and Memory<T>?
cards.h: A window onto memory, not a copy.
s: Span of T is a view over a block of memory, like part of an array or a string, without copying it. So I can slice and parse data with no extra allocations. It lives only on the stack, so it can't be used in async methods. Memory of T is the version that can be stored on the heap and used across awaits. They are useful in hot paths like parsing large CSV files.

cards.q: Response caching vs output caching vs IMemoryCache vs HybridCache?
cards.h: Headers for clients, outputs for endpoints, data for code.
s: Response caching uses HTTP cache headers so browsers and proxies can cache responses. Output caching, added in .NET 7, stores the response on the server and gives me control to expire it. cards.q: How does JWT bearer authentication work in the ASP.NET Core pipeline?
cards.h: Authentication reads the badge; authorization checks the door list.
s: The client sends the JWT in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. The authentication middleware validates it: the signature using the identity provider's public key, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. If it is valid, it creates the user with claims, and the authorization middleware checks policies and roles for the endpoint. If it fails, we return 401, and if the user lacks permission, 403.

cards.q: What are System.Threading.Channels?
cards.h: An in-process queue with a full-sign.
s: Channels are a fast, thread-safe queue for passing data between producers and consumers in the same process, and they work with async. A bounded channel has a size limit, so producers wait when it is full, which gives back-pressure. I use them with a BackgroundService: the API writes work into the channel and the background worker processes it, so the request returns quickly.

Instead of calling DateTime.UtcNow directly, I inject TimeProvider, so in tests I can use a fake time provider and move time forward. script: Thank you. I'm Pradeep, a backend-focused full-stack engineer with about five and a half years of experience, mainly in C# and .NET.

For the last four years I've been at IQVIA, working on IRT. IRT is a regulated clinical-trial platform that handles patient randomization, drug supply, shipment tracking and eConsent for global trials. Because it's GxP regulated, every change we make has to be tested, traceable and auditable, and that has shaped how I work.

Day to day, I design and build .NET microservices and ASP.NET Core Web APIs with EF Core and SQL Server, and I also build Node.js and Python services and React components. Our services run on AWS, on ECS, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB and RDS, with Terraform and CloudFormation, Docker, and Azure DevOps pipelines.

The work I'm proudest of is an internal MCP server that I designed and built on my own. It exposes about 77 tools for builds, releases and multi-node deployments to AI agents. That cut our deployment time from 6 hours to 2, and the people needed per deployment from 6 to 1, and I packaged it so my teammates install and use it.

I also own production issues. For example, I root-caused a RabbitMQ outage and fixed it with publisher confirms, and I delivered security fixes for token-based logout, SSO cookie failures and reverse tabnabbing. I've delivered features end to end too, like a CSV bulk import that is live in production and a study-transfer safety guard.
Before IQVIA, I started my career at DXC Technology, building C# and .NET Framework solutions on SharePoint.
Now I'm looking for a senior backend role where I can own the design and delivery of scalable services, and keep using AI tools to help the team move faster. That's why this role interests me.
